summary: Aluminum grain-size engineering and silicon dielectric-edge trimming both suppress loss in superconducting coplanar waveguide resonators, improving quality factors from $6 \times 10^4$ to $2.3 \times 10^6$ on high-resistivity silicon. Substrate heating during $200$ nm aluminum deposition increases grain size to $1.2$ µm and reduces non-TLS loss, while a two-step "Tropic" etch (SF$_6$ followed by CHF$_3$) smooths silicon surfaces and suppresses TLS loss.
motivation: Material losses in superconducting circuits limit qubit $T_1$ and resonator quality factors; understanding how intrinsic superconductor microstructure and dielectric-edge roughness drive TLS and non-TLS loss mechanisms has remained poorly characterized.
method: Aluminum films ($200$ nm) were deposited at four substrate temperatures ($25$–$300$ °C) on high-resistivity silicon ($\rho \geq 10$ kΩ·cm), with grain sizes characterized by AFM and cross-sectional STEM-EDS. Silicon etching variants (unetched, anisotropic CHF$_3$, and hybrid SF$_6$/CHF$_3$ Tropic profiles) were applied to $\lambda/4$ CPW resonators, with single-photon quality factors measured at $10$ mK via vector-network-analyzer reflection.
result: Non-TLS loss decreased from $Q_i \approx 4 \times 10^4$ to $4.2 \times 10^5$ with $300$ °C deposition (grain boundaries reduced, no oxide detected at boundaries by EDS); TLS loss further suppressed by dielectric trimming, reaching $Q_i = 2.3 \times 10^6$ with the smooth-sidewall Stropic profile, operating at $6.5$–$8.1$ GHz where TLS loss is most pronounced.
